messages.body_plain:
Hi Nick,

I have used a starting tree in BEAST to , and  eventually I ran BioGeoBEARS on the maximum clade credibility tree.
My question is do you think I need to run the model across multiple trees again?  If yes can i do it for 10 trees randomly sampled acorss the posterior since i dont have acess to much powerful computers here. ( I used a starting tree prior assuming that there wont be much topological uncertainties ). Do you think this approach is correct?

Looking forward to hearing form you.

Regards,
Sandy

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Running biogeobears on multiple trees
messages.body_plain:
Hi!  Like anything, it's a cost-benefit calculation: what do you get from the extra work involved?

My basic thought is: don't do a multiple-trees run "just because" or because of some abstract sense of nervousness or "other people do it" or "more is always better in papers" or "some reviewer might suggest I do multiple trees just-because or because-other-people-do-it or whatever".

*If* you have substantial tree uncertainty and *if* its in a region of the tree where it might effect some important biogeographical inference, then sure, do it.  If (as is common) you're just going to smush all the individual tree biogeography analyses back onto some summary tree anyway, then I don't see too much point.

I've posted some further thoughts at:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/biogeobears/M8zw8Kidseo

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/biogeobears/kASdtlF2bu8

Cheers!
Nick

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] BSM event tables
messages.body_plain:
Hi!  I'm not sure I understand the question?

The table has "from" on the left, and "to" on the top.

So, row A, column D represents the average number of dispersal events from A->D
And row D, column A represents the average number of dispersal events from D->A

Note that even when the range history is, say, ABC -> ABCD (a "d" event, range expansion), the actual dispersal event is modeled as coming from one of the 3 areas (A, B, or C), so the ABC->ABCD event will (1/3 of the time in the simplest case) actually represent a A->D dispersal event.

Other tables give the standard deviation in these event counts, divide up the events (d events versus j events, etc.), etc.

Cheers,
Nick

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Re: changing colors in BioGeoBEARS
messages.body_plain:
Hi -- running out the door, but briefly, you would add a line like this to the script:

colors_list_for_states  = c("white", "red", "green", "blue")
# (that would be for a 4-state problem)

# For 350 states:
colors_list_for_states  = c("white", "red", "green", "blue", rep("grey50", times=346))
# ...which repeats "grey50" for the last 346 colors

# Look at the colors list:
colors_list_for_states

# Then you add the colors list to the plot_BioGeoBEARS_results command:

# States
res2 = plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(results_object, analysis_titletxt, addl_params=list("j"), plotwhat="text", label.offset=0.45, tipcex=0.7, statecex=0.7, splitcex=0.6, titlecex=0.8, plotsplits=TRUE, cornercoords_loc=scriptdir, include_null_range=TRUE, tr=tr, tipranges=tipranges, colors_list_for_states=colors_list_for_states)

# Pie chart
plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(results_object, analysis_titletxt, addl_params=list("j"), plotwhat="pie", label.offset=0.45, tipcex=0.7, statecex=0.7, splitcex=0.6, titlecex=0.8, plotsplits=TRUE, cornercoords_loc=scriptdir, include_null_range=TRUE, tr=tr, tipranges=tipranges, colors_list_for_states=colors_list_for_states)

Cheers,
Nick

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Model Test: stratified x non-stratified analises - Does i t make sense at all?
messages.subject_clean: [BioGeoBEARS] Model Test: stratified x non-stratified analises - Does i t make sense at all?
messages.body_plain:
Hi- on iPhone but:

The data are the ranges at the tips of the tree (and implicitly the tree can be thought of as data, but we are not calculating its likelihood unless we add a Yule process likelihood). These data are the same whether the analysis is time-stratified or not. Time-stratified models are just another set of model variants.

Comparing the fit of stratified and non-stratified models to this same data is therefore fine and can be done with AICc. However the Likelihood Ratio Test is not appropriate, as stratified and non-stratified models are not nested. The manual dispersal multipliers are not free parameters - you will have to learn the difference between free and fixed parameters for any of this to make sense. When AIC etc count parameters, they are counting *free* parameters.

The +w model variant is a way to make models with and without dispersal multipliers nested, if used properly, as then w is a free parameter, and when w=0 all dispersal multipliers convert to 1.0 - see Dupin et al 2017, J Biogeog.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Model Test: stratified x non-stratified analises - Does i t make sense at all?
messages.subject_clean: [BioGeoBEARS] Model Test: stratified x non-stratified analises - Does i t make sense at all?
messages.body_plain:
Hi -- typically you would report the AICcs, model weights etc. for all models tested, since they were all in your initial set of a priori reasonable models to test -- this would be the usual advice from Burnham & Anderson (2002 and various other publications: http://phylo.wikidot.com/advice-on-statistical-model-comparison-in-biogeobears#refs )

Usually these are presented in a table in the paper.

You can also calculate the model weights for just the pair of models, this is a measure of the relative fit of the two models compared to each other.  However it would be a bit misleading if, say, your model weights were:

DEC - 15%
DIVALIKE - 10%
all others together - 75%

...to then just report the DEC and DIVALIKE model weights as 60% vs 40%.

If (as is common but not universal), only DEC+J and DIVALIKE+J received much weight, then it makes little difference if the models receiving 0.001% of the model weight are included -- but you should include them for thoroughness, since you tested them.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.subject: Trimming tips in areas outside of focal study to save computation time
messages.subject_clean: Trimming tips in areas outside of focal study to save computation time
messages.body_plain:
Dear Dr. Matzke,

I am preparing to set up a BioGeoBEARS analysis on a very large phylogeny of ~12,000 species. I am interested in transitions among freshwater realms across the whole tree, even though the overall clade also contains many marine species. I have six freshwater areas of interest, and a 7th area that is "restricted to marine", meaning absence from the first six areas. At least half of the species in this phylogeny belong to the "marine" category. Marine and freshwater categories show reasonably strong conservatism, with some subclades having no transitions among realms, and some having many transitions. My interest is in the timing and frequency of transitions among freshwater areas, say Neotropics and Afrotropics. Marine groups represent one possible intermediate transition between freshwater realms, and are not otherwise of interest in my study.

Since the starting phylogeny is so large, I am exploring options to cut down tips in the "marine" category to save on computation time. I have thought of three options, though you may have other suggestions: (1) Keep phylogeny as-is, with ~6,000 tips coded as "marine". (2) Trim marine clades down to only 1 tip per clade, unless they have freshwater species nested within them. (3) Only analyze separate subclades in the phylogeny that are predominately freshwater, then combine results later on.

I am worried about how the latter two approaches may bias my results. Would you expect the trimming described above to dramatically change the inferred transition timing in other clades? Do you have any other concerns I haven't thought of?

Thank you for your help!
Best,
Liz Miller
